newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Rebel Chechnya waits to learn who is new leader.
newsitem.headline: Rebel Chechnya waits to learn who is new leader.

text.p: Chechnya's war-weary voters waited on Tuesday to find out who had won presidential and parliamentary elections as ballots were collected and counted across the mountainous Moslem region.

The elections on Monday are a crucial step in restoring order and stability in a land still heavily scarred by 21 months of fierce fighting between Russian troops and rebel guerrillas bent on proclaiming Chechnya a fully independent state.

Early reports suggested a high turnout and polling stations were kept open two hours later than initially planned, to 10 p.m. (1900 GMT), to cope with the flow. Some voters were still waiting to vote inside the stations at around 11 p.m.
Outside, on the freezing streets of the Chechen capital Grozny, armed policemen on the alert for any sign of trouble warmed their hands over burning truck tyres.
The Central Election Commission has declared the poll valid, saying well over the required 50 percent of eligible voters had cast their ballots.

Reuters reporters who questioned hundreds of voters in various districts across Chechnya said Aslan Maskhadov, the former guerrilla commander, appeared to be well ahead of his rivals in the race for the presidency.
Maskhadov, who led the rebels' delegation in peace talks with Moscow last summer, needs to clear the 50 percent barrier to avoid a run-off ballot in two weeks' time.
"I see our land flourishing under Maskhadov. He has more experience (than the others)," said one elderly man dressed in a a handmade sheepskin coat, after casting his vote.
Maskhadov, 45, has pledged to "bring order" to Chechnya as his first step and to develop normal ties with Russia.
Like all the main contenders in the 13-man field, however, Maskhadov has vowed to turn Chechnya's de facto independence won in the war into sovereignty.
President Boris Yeltsin, who admits that sending troops to crush Chechen secession in 1994 was a mistake, agreed to the elections as part of a face-saving peace.
But the Kremlin opposes outright independence for fear of unsettling its southern frontier and fuelling other ethnic conflicts.
Russian Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov said last week that Moscow should send troops back into Chechnya if ethnic Russians still living there came under attack.
On Monday Kulikov, a strong opponent of Chechen independence, announced Russia was stepping up the police presence along its border with the breakaway region.

Over 100 foreign observers are in Chechnya to monitor an election for the first time. Several observers from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) said they were impressed by the smoothness of the process.
Tim Guldimann, who heads the OSCE mission, said the high turnout was "a very positive sign". None of the observers had any trouble. Chechen officials had feared for their safety.
Journalists saw some minor infringements but there was little sign of intimidation of voters and remarkably few guns were in evidence for a region still awash with weaponry.
The other main contenders for the presidency are acting president Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev and guerrilla leader Shamil Basayev, who is wanted in Russia for "terrorism".
Basayev, 32, who made his name with a bloody raid on a Russian town in 1995, forecast his own victory and said Russia would "collapse" if it did not accept Chechen independence.
He also said that, win or lose, he hoped for good relations with other separatist leaders. But he later accused Maskhadov of surrounding himself with "criminals".
The first results may come overnight. Some 850 candidates are also standing for 63 local assembly seats.
